extracted.intended_audience: media/journalism scholars and researchers studying global television news content
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic content-analysis framework for evaluating how ‘global’ television newscasts are, including sampling procedures, headline/item coding, country/location coding, and speaking-actor coding to map topics, geography and voices in global broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global checkbox ("global-as-issue")
rubrics_metrics.description: A “global” checkbox was ticked if a headline or news item related to a global issue (such as terror, a pandemic, environmental or refugee crisis); if it was framed in global terms (e.g., “the world came one step closer to winning the battle against COVID-19 this week when …”); if it was about the foreign affairs of an intergovernmental organization (such as the EU, Arab League or African Union) or the actions of NATO or the UN (such as a General Assembly meeting) or about the UN taking a stance for cosmopolitan principles; if it concerned the actions of the International Criminal Court; or if it was about a global diaspora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding criteria for the global checkbox were reviewed continuously over a year; coders were warned this was the most difficult coding category and examples prompted re-evaluation. The study refers to this operationalization as “global-as-issue.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline coding (top-of-broadcast metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines of broadcasts were coded because they are repeated, often catch viewers' attention and provide evidence of frames; many viewers catch the headlines and little else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One broadcast per channel per week was sampled (15 Sep 2008–30 Jun 2020, except 2010). Headline coding allows efficient analysis of a large corpus with a high degree of inter-coder reliability and is used to compute measures like percentage of global headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: News item coding (full-item metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entire news items (full broadcasts) were coded to obtain more detailed information, especially about who speaks in the reports (speaking actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second sample included the full Monday broadcasts for two years (2011 and 2015), yielding 5379 items coded; this provides a complementary check to headline findings (items sometimes show a higher share of global content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of global headlines/items
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion (percentage) of headlines or items coded as dealing with “global” issues (based on the global checkbox) is used as a primary metric of how 'global' a channel's newsworld is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percentages were calculated across years and channels (examples given: averages between 7.6% and 9.2% across channels; spikes in 2020). Used to compare channels and periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of newsworld (# of countries mentioned)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many different countries feature in the headlines (a measure of how 'big' the channel's newsworld is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coders chose from a list of officially recognized states (tweaked with additional options). Results used to compare channels (e.g., AJE consistently the biggest; CNNI smallest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-frequency / top-country ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Which countries occur most frequently in headlines/items (used to assess geographic bias or dominance, e.g., US prevalence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to test assumptions about Western/Anglo-Saxon dominance and to reveal differences between channels' geographic attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global option in country list (location coding rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific 'global' country/location option selected when the event involved inter-regional or worldwide involvement, two or more regions from different continents, or more than five countries from at least two different continents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'global' location option differs from 'global-as-issue' (topic-based) and captures events whose location is trans-regional or not attributable to a single state; coders could make up to three country/location selections per item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Up to three country/location selections per item
rubrics_metrics.description: Coders were permitted to select up to three countries (or the global option) to capture multi-location reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows complex items to be associated with multiple states/regions; supports analysis of inter-regional involvement and breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking-actor inclusion rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Only actors who spoke in news items were coded; people who were seen but not heard were not coded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: speaking actors potentially have a power of definition that silent actors do not; coding speakers focuses on who is given voice in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking-actor roles list (30 categories) and role assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Coders used an extensive list of 30 speaking-actor categories and could assign up to two roles per person who spoke (e.g., head of government, representative of an IGO, refugee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role assignments recorded for each speaking actor and later collapsed for analysis; detailed categories enable later grouping into thematic categories (elites, civil society, ordinary people, refugees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor metadata: gender, language/dubbing, identification
rubrics_metrics.description: For each speaking actor coded, coders noted the gender of the actor, whether they spoke English or were dubbed, and whether or not they were identified by name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to examine visibility, anonymity (e.g., ordinary people anonymized vs named elites), and language practices (dubbing) in global news narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate actor categories (elites / civil society / ordinary people / refugees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking-actor categories were collapsed into thematic groupings — elites, civil society, ordinary people, refugees — to analyse whose voices dominate global news reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example findings: elites account for roughly 71–77% of speaking actors across channels; ordinary people and civil society vary by channel. Use these aggregates to compare channels' inclusivity of voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts-as-subcategory metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts were extracted from the 'elites' category and treated separately to capture the frequency of expert voices (used to indicate strategic narration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example finding: RT uses experts extensively (e.g., 30% of speaking actors), which can indicate strategic narrative techniques; analysts are advised to display experts separately when studying voice and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling procedure: one evening newscast per week
rubrics_metrics.description: The sample comprised one broadcast by each channel, every week, across the study period (15 Sep 2008–30 Jun 2020, except 2010) chosen to reflect a European primetime evening newscast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges schedule changes and practical difficulties; the weekly evening program is treated as a systematic 'probe' into routine packaging rather than exhaustive coverage of all programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal span and sub-sample design
rubrics_metrics.description: Longitudinal sampling across 13 years for headlines (2008–2020 excluding 2010) with a second, more detailed sample of whole broadcasts for two years (2011, 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to avoid snapshot bias and to allow both broad temporal trends and more detailed voice analysis; allows comparison across crises (e.g., 2011, 2014, 2020).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding team, reliability practice, and data workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: A bespoke coding database was used by a team of 20 coders of 14 nationalities; raw data were exported to SPSS for summarization and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coders rotated channels and periods to facilitate comparability and avoid immersion effects; continuous review of coding criteria and team composition aimed to improve inter-coder reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contours of the newsworld: topic + geographic scope + voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'contours' of a channel's newsworld are operationalized by combining topic coding (global-as-issue), geographic spread (# countries mentioned / global location), and who populates the newsworld (speaking actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multi-dimensional approach is used to determine how 'global' a channel's reporting is and to compare channels beyond simple topic counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and narrative-stage follow-up (qualitative complement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative 'what' coding is supplemented (or recommended to be supplemented) by qualitative analysis of framing and narratives ('how') to fully assess discursive connections and cosmopolitan outlooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that coding the 'how' (framing, narrative structure) is necessary to complete the picture and that quantitative findings should be followed by qualitative discourse analysis and production/audience studies for explanation.
